title: The inner critic
hookLine: Paul Gilbert's compassion-focused therapy works with harsh self-criticism

lines: A VOICE NO FRIEND WOULD USE.
cards: "Idiot." One word, said under the breath, after the keys get locked in the car, or after the email goes out with the wrong name in it. Nobody else heard it.
Nobody else needed to. It's a voice some people carry around, and it can talk to them in a way they would never talk to a friend, or a child, or even a stranger on the bus.
After days of kindness moving outward, today looks inward, at the one relationship where kindness can be hardest to pass on.

teach.b: First, a therapist who took the voice seriously. The British psychologist Paul Gilbert developed what he calls compassion-focused therapy, working with people whose self-criticism was harsh and stubborn.
He noticed that some of them understood perfectly well that they deserved kindness, and still couldn't feel any of it toward themselves. Second, his map.

Gilbert describes three broad systems for handling emotion: one for threat, which watches for danger; one for drive, which chases goals; and one for soothing, which settles us when we're safe and cared for.
In his account, a harsh inner critic keeps the threat system switched on. You become both the attacker and the one under attack. Third, the work.

Gilbert's approach doesn't try to argue the critic into silence. It builds up the soothing side: a warmer tone of voice, a slower breath, and imagining what a wise, kind presence would say about the same mistake.
The point isn't to stop caring about doing better; it's to change who's doing the talking. Fourth, an old line this path met on day four hundred thirty-nine.

In a letter to his friend Lucilius, the Stoic Seneca passes on a saying from the philosopher Hecato, in Gummere's words: "I have begun to be a friend to myself." Seneca treats that as real progress. Not finished.
Begun. A friend tells you the truth about the locked car, and doesn't call you an idiot while doing it.

how: In compassion-focused therapy, people practice meeting their own mistakes with a warm inner voice, often by imagining what a kind, wise companion would say. Some contemplative traditions have their own versions of the same turn toward oneself.

o: the harsh voice inside that attacks your own mistakes
a reviewer who judges books and films for a living
a wise conscience that always tells the plain truth

games.q: the inner critic: tap the pairs.

s: in Gilbert's approach, the goal is to argue the critic into silence
it builds up the soothing side instead: a warmer voice, a slower breath.
Gilbert noticed some people understood they deserved kindness but couldn't feel it toward themselves
that gap is part of what his therapy works with.
being kinder to yourself means you stop caring about doing better
the point is to change who's doing the talking, not to stop caring.

games.q: you've just sent an email with the wrong name in it. the critic starts up. what do you try?
o: tell yourself it doesn't matter at all.
ask what a kind, wise friend would say about it.
let the critic finish, since it's probably right.
games.why: Gilbert's approach builds a warm voice that can tell the truth kindly, rather than denying the mistake or giving in to the attack.

practice: Let the out-breath grow a little longer than the in-breath, and recall one recent moment when the critic spoke, hearing its exact words only briefly.
Then imagine someone wise and kind beside you, real or imagined, and let them say something true about that moment, not "it was perfect", in a warm tone, so their words are the last ones.

wordCard.voice: The inner critic. The harsh voice inside, which Paul Gilbert's therapy answers by building up warmth instead of more attack. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: softer inside. Honest and kind can live in the very same voice. Gently does it.

sources.ref: Paul Gilbert, The Compassionate Mind, and his papers on compassion-focused therapy
Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 6
sources.q: I have begun to be a friend to myself.
